newsitem.title: ROMANIA: S.Korea's Daewoo defends Romania venture.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Daewoo defends Romania venture.

text.p: A venture of South Korea's Daewoo Heavy Industries in Romania rejected as pointless on Thursday plans announced by the country's second most senior official to launch a probe into Daewoo's investments in Romania.

"We fulfilled all our obligations stipulated in the accords. Such investigations are not necessary," Radu Andrei, head of the public relations department at Rodae SA car maker said from the city of Craiova.

His remarks referred to reports in the local media quoting Petre Roman, chairman of the upper Senate of the Romanian parliament, as saying the government would start an "analysis" into the way Daewoo had fulfilled its commitments in Rodae.
Roman was reported to have made the remarks during a visit on Wednesday to a Daewoo-owned car plant in the city of Pitesti.
Daewoo has said it would commit $156 million for its 51 percent share in the venture.

Roman was quoted as saying that if investigations revealed discrepancies between Daewoo's initial commitments and reality that were against Romania's interests, then "one could ask serious questions about this cooperation".
Roman could not be reached for comment but his spokeswoman Rodica Georgescu told Reuters, "Mr Roman has been accurately quoted by the press reports."
Rodae was created as a joint venture between Daewoo and the state Automobile Craiova car maker in 1994, when Romania's former leftist government allowed Daewoo to import tax-free 20,000 of its cars.

Critics of the Daewoo deal said a special foreign investment law granting extra tax benefits to firms investing over $50 million in industry was pushed through parliament before the accord was signed to facilitate the deal.
The deal was done under the previous leftist government which lost office in elections last November.
Government officials were not available to confirm whether such an investigation had actually been launched.
European Union car makers protested against Daewoo securing tax-free access for $140 million worth of its cars. The EU told Romania the move was discriminatory against EU car producers.
But Daewoo rejected the accusations, saying the move was justified by the size of its Romanian investment, which it said would amount to some $1.0 billion by year 2000.

If the planned investigation showed that Daewoo's cash contribution for its 51 percent stake in Rodae consisted of earnings from the sale of the 20,000 cars it imported tax-free, then "the Romanian state was cheated", Roman was quoted as saying in a variety of newspapers.

"Daewoo offered us the (20,000) cars as a credit. We spent the money from their sale to solve administrative problems," a Dong Kyu Park, president of Daewoo Automobile Romania (DAR), said in a letter to authorities this week.
The sales had been vital for Rodae to secure payment of its employees and maintain staff levels, the letter said.
A Daewoo statement on Thursday said the company planned to invest a further $450 million in the Craiova plant this year.
